questions.question: What does the continuum hypothesis assert?
options: $\aleph_0$ and $\mathfrak{c}$ are the same cardinality.
Every infinite set has cardinality $\aleph_0$ or $\mathfrak{c}$.
No cardinality lies strictly between $\aleph_0$ and $\mathfrak{c}$.
No set has cardinality strictly larger than $\mathfrak{c}$.

questions.question: What kind of set would refute the continuum hypothesis?
options: A set $A$ with $\aleph_0 \le \operatorname{card}(A) \le \mathfrak{c}$
A set $A$ with $\operatorname{card}(A) \gt \mathfrak{c}$
A set $A$ with $\aleph_0 \lt \operatorname{card}(A) \lt \mathfrak{c}$
A set $A$ with $\operatorname{card}(A) \lt \aleph_0$

questions.question: Does a set of cardinality $\mathfrak{c}$ violate the continuum hypothesis?
options: Yes. Every uncountable set violates the continuum hypothesis.
Yes. $\mathfrak{c}$ is strictly above $\aleph_0$, which is enough.
No. $\mathfrak{c}$ is the upper endpoint, not strictly between.
No. The hypothesis only concerns sets smaller than $\aleph_0$.

questions.question: Why do $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ not by themselves settle the continuum hypothesis?
options: $\mathbb{Q}$ is $\aleph_0$ and $\mathbb{R}$ is $\mathfrak{c}$, so they only show the endpoints.
$\mathbb{Q}$ has cardinality strictly between $\aleph_0$ and $\mathfrak{c}$.
$\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ both have cardinality $\mathfrak{c}$, so no gap can appear.
The hypothesis concerns subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, not $\mathbb{Q}$ or $\mathbb{R}$.

questions.question: Assume the continuum hypothesis. If $A$ is infinite and $\operatorname{card}(A) \lt \mathfrak{c}$, what must be true about $A$?
options: $\operatorname{card}(A)=\aleph_0$
$A$ must be finite
$\aleph_0 \lt \operatorname{card}(A) \lt \mathfrak{c}$
$\operatorname{card}(A)=\mathfrak{c}$

questions.question: Why does Cantor's theorem alone not answer the continuum hypothesis?
options: It gives only $\aleph_0\le\mathfrak{c}$, not a strict inequality between them.
It shows $\aleph_0 \lt \mathfrak{c}$, not whether a cardinality lies between.
It shows that $2^{\mathfrak{c}}$ lies strictly between $\aleph_0$ and $\mathfrak{c}$.
It applies only to finite sets, not to infinite sets such as $\mathbb{N}$.

questions.question: Assume the continuum hypothesis. What are the possible cardinalities of a subset $A\subseteq\mathbb{R}$?
options: Only $\aleph_0$
Finite cardinality, $\aleph_0$, or $\mathfrak{c}$
Only $\mathfrak{c}$
Only cardinalities strictly between $\aleph_0$ and $\mathfrak{c}$

questions.question: Let $\aleph_1$ be the smallest cardinality larger than $\aleph_0$. Which statement is equivalent to the continuum hypothesis?
options: $\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_1$
$\mathfrak{c}=\aleph_0$
$\aleph_1\le\mathfrak{c}$
$\aleph_1<\mathfrak{c}$

questions.question: Assume the axioms of ZFC (Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice) are consistent. What is the status of the continuum hypothesis relative to ZFC?
options: ZFC proves it, via Cantor's diagonal argument
ZFC refutes it, since $2^{\mathbb{R}}$ is larger than $\mathfrak{c}$
ZFC can neither prove nor refute it
It is open only because no proof has been found yet
